title: LRU cache with TTL
label: idb
statement:
Implement an LRU Cache with TTL expiry.

It is similar to a standard LRU but each entry has a time-to-live.

get() should return -1 if the key has expired even if it is still in the cache.

How would you handle cleanup of expired entries without impacting get() latency?

Discuss: lazy eviction, background cleanup, trade-offs, complexity, concurrency, memory implications.

flaw.ctx: You asked for TTL. The expiry test passes.
flaw.answer: Expired entries are **never removed**: Get returns -1 but leaves them in the map and list. They count toward capacity, so the next Put evicts a *live* LRU entry while the dead one stays. Keys that are never read again stay forever — unbounded growth in a long-running process.
flaw.fix: Remove on an expired read; prefer expired victims at eviction; add a bounded sweep (see LruTtlCache).

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.
O(1) `Remove(node)`, `AddFirst`, `RemoveLast` given a `LinkedListNode<T>` handle. Storing the handle in the dictionary avoids an O(n) search.
No. Concurrent `Remove`/`AddFirst` corrupts its pointers (R3 corrupted in 20/20 runs).

Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).
Each single call: `TryAdd`, `TryRemove`, `TryUpdate` (compare-and-swap on the value), `TryGetValue`, the indexer. `AddOrUpdate`/`GetOrAdd` atomically *store* — but see the next question.

qa.q: Does a read take a lock?
qa.a: No — reads are lock-free. Writes lock one stripe of buckets (lock striping), not the whole table. `Count` and `ToArray` take *all* the locks, so avoid them on a hot path.

qa.q: Is a read-modify-write across two calls safe?
qa.a: No. `TryGetValue` then `d[k] = v + 1` is check-then-act (debugging exercise D4 lost ~80% of increments). Use `AddOrUpdate`, or a `TryUpdate` loop.

qa.q: Do GetOrAdd / AddOrUpdate run the factory once?
qa.a: Not guaranteed: the delegate runs outside the lock and can run on several racing threads; only one result is stored. For an expensive factory, store `Lazy<T>` (review exercise R8).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Implement an LRU Cache with TTL expiry.
> 
> It is similar to a standard LRU but each entry has a time-to-live.
> 
> get() should return -1 if the key has expired even if it is still in the cache.

**Given with it:** How would you handle cleanup of expired entries without impacting get() latency?

Discuss: lazy eviction, background cleanup, trade-offs, complexity, concurrency, memory implications.

A cache that forgets things for two different reasons at once. It forgets the least-recently-used entry because it is full, and it forgets any entry whose clock has run out. Those are independent, and that is the whole difficulty: capacity is about ordering, expiry is about time, and the two do not agree on who should go first.

Three operations. `Get(key)` returns the value, or -1 if the key is absent **or** expired. `Put(key, value, ttl)` inserts or updates, renewing the expiry. And under the covers, eviction picks a victim when the cache is full.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
Two things the statement leaves open, and both change code.

**1. Is the TTL per entry or per cache?** "each entry has a time-to-live" reads as per entry, so `Put` takes a TTL. If it is one TTL for the whole cache it is a constructor argument, and the expiry field per node becomes just the insertion time.

**2. Does an expired entry still occupy capacity?** "even if it is still in the cache" says yes — expiry is logical, not physical. That single sentence is what forces lazy expiry and is why the follow-up about cleanup exists at all.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| TTL is supplied per entry, on `Put`. | If it is one cache-wide TTL, the constructor takes it and the node stores an insertion time instead. Two lines different; ask rather than guess. |
| A re-`Put` of an existing key **renews** the TTL. | If it must not, an update has to preserve the original expiry, and a hot key can then expire mid-use — which is sometimes exactly what you want for a session cache. |
| Expiry is inclusive: an entry with `expiresAt == now` is dead. | One character in the comparison. Whichever you pick, say it, because a test will sit exactly on that boundary. |
| Single-threaded unless told otherwise. | Under concurrency the doubly linked list is the problem, not the dictionary: two threads relinking the same neighbours corrupt it silently. See the follow-up. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
Start from what has to be O(1) and work backwards — do not start from "use a HashMap".

Eviction needs to find the least-recently-used entry and remove it in constant time. A dictionary can find a node instantly but has no idea which one is oldest. An array knows the order but costs O(n) to move an element to the front. Neither structure can do both, so you hold both: a **doubly linked list** for the order, and a **dictionary from key to the list node**. The list gives O(1) reordering *provided you already have the node*, and the dictionary is what gives you the node. That pairing is the answer to plain LRU.

Now the TTL. The tempting move is a second ordered structure keyed on expiry, so you can find the next entry to die. Resist it for a moment and ask what the requirement actually says: `Get` must return -1 for an expired key. It does **not** say the entry must be gone. So the cheapest correct implementation is to check the expiry of the one entry you already hold, on the path where you already hold it — **lazy expiry**. One comparison, no new structure, no background work.

That is the key observation, and it generalises: *a deadline you only have to honour when someone looks does not need a timer.* The expiry heap only becomes necessary when the requirement changes from "return -1" to "reclaim the memory", which is precisely what the supplied follow-up asks.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Keep a `List<(key, value, expiresAt, lastUsed)>`. On `Get`, scan for the key; if found and live, stamp `lastUsed` with a counter and return it. On `Put` when full, scan for the smallest `lastUsed` and remove it. *`Get` O(n), `Put` O(n), space O(capacity). Every operation is a linear scan.*

**Why not good enough.** It is not that O(n) is slow at capacity 100. It is that a cache exists to be faster than the thing behind it, and an O(n) cache has a cost that grows with its own hit rate — the bigger you make it to improve the hit rate, the slower each hit becomes. The design is self-defeating, which is a better answer than "linear is bad".

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `Get(key)` / `Put(key, value, ttl)`, plus an injectable clock |
| TRANSFORMATION | Every entry becomes a list node carrying the key, the value and an **absolute** expiry time. Absolute, not remaining — remaining would have to be decremented. |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `Dictionary<int, Node>` for lookup, plus a doubly linked list with head and tail sentinels for recency order |
| ALGORITHM | Lookup in the dictionary; check expiry; on a live hit move the node to the front; on overflow unlink the node before the tail sentinel |
| OUTPUT | The value, or -1 for absent or expired |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- `Get`: dictionary lookup. Miss → -1.
- Compare `_clock() >= node.ExpiresAt`. Dead → unlink, remove from the dictionary, return -1. Reclaiming it here is free, because you are already holding the node.
- Live → move the node to the front and return its value.
- `Put`: if the key exists, overwrite the value, reset `ExpiresAt`, move to front, done.
- Otherwise, if at capacity, take `_tail.Prev` — the least recently used — unlink it and drop its key.
- Create the node, insert it in the dictionary, link it at the front.

- Both operations should be **O(1)**. That rules out scanning for an expired entry on the hot path.
- An expired entry is still physically present until something removes it, so `Count` and capacity are counted in entries, not in *live* entries.
- The clock has to be injectable, or the behaviour is untestable. Passing `Func<long>` in the constructor costs nothing and is the difference between a design you can test and one you can only hope about.
- Time is monotonic. If it is not — an NTP step backwards — entries can appear to un-expire. Use a monotonic source, not wall-clock.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `Dictionary<int, Node>` | O(1) key → node. Storing the **node**, not the value, is the whole trick: it is what lets the list be reordered without searching it. |
| Doubly linked list | O(1) unlink of a node you already hold. Singly linked will not do it — you would need the predecessor, which costs a scan. |
| Head and tail sentinels | Removes every null check from `Unlink` and `LinkFront`. This is not tidiness; the null-handling is where hand-written LRU actually breaks under time pressure. |
| An absolute `ExpiresAt` on the node | Comparing two longs is the entire expiry check, and it works no matter how long the entry has sat there. |
| No expiry-ordered structure, on purpose | Correctness does not need one. Adding it before the requirement demands it is the most common over-engineering in this question. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**Why the node holds the key as well as the value.** When eviction picks `_tail.Prev`, it has a node and needs to delete the matching dictionary entry — which needs the key. Without `Node.Key` there is no way back from the list to the dictionary, and this is the single most common omission in a first attempt.

**The invariant, stated once.** The dictionary and the list hold **exactly the same set of entries** at every point between operations. Every mutation touches both. `Remove` exists precisely so that pairing cannot drift: there is one function that unlinks and deletes, and nothing else does either alone.

**Why `Get` is allowed to mutate.** On an expired hit it unlinks and removes. That is not a side effect smuggled in; it is the cheapest possible reclamation, because the node is already in hand. It also means the cache self-cleans along whatever access pattern it actually has — hot keys get checked often, cold keys sit until they are evicted by capacity.

**Why eviction never scans.** `EvictOne` could look for an already-expired victim and prefer it, which would be nicer. It would also be O(capacity), and the stated requirement is O(1). Keeping the eviction strictly at `_tail.Prev` preserves the bound; the scan belongs in the sweeper, where it is bounded and off the hot path.

**The bug the sentinels prevent.** Without sentinels, `Unlink` needs four null checks and `LinkFront` needs two, and the case that breaks is removing the only node — head and tail both have to be updated. With sentinels, `n.Prev` and `n.Next` are never null, so the four-line version is correct for every case including the last one.

**What `Count` deliberately does not tell you.** It counts entries, including expired ones not yet reclaimed. A `LiveCount` would have to walk the whole list. If a metric is needed, count reclamations instead — a counter is O(1), a census is not.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Get` | O(1) | O(1) | One dictionary probe, one comparison, two pointer swaps |
| `Put` | O(1) | O(1) | One probe; eviction is `_tail.Prev`, never a search |
| eviction | O(1) | O(1) | The victim is always the node before the tail sentinel |
| `Sweep(budget)` | O(k log n) | O(n) heap | k reclaimed, each a heap pop; the heap holds one record per `Put` |
| overall space | — | O(capacity) | One node and one dictionary entry per held key |

**All O(1) here means expected, not worst case**, because the dictionary is a hash table. The list operations are genuinely worst-case O(1); the hashing is not. It is a small distinction and a real one, and saying it unprompted reads very differently from being corrected on it.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `capacity <= 0` | Throws in the constructor. A zero-capacity cache that silently accepts `Put` and always misses is worse than a loud failure. |
| `Get` on a key never inserted | Dictionary miss → -1, nothing mutated. |
| TTL of 0 | Expires immediately, since `expiresAt == now` and the check is `>=`. It still occupies a slot until something reclaims it — worth stating. |
| Negative TTL | Already expired on arrival. Accepted as written; if the interviewer wants a throw, that is one line, but say which you chose. |
| Re-`Put` of an existing key when full | No eviction, because the count does not change. Getting this wrong evicts a live entry for nothing. |
| Every entry expired | `Get` reclaims them one at a time as they are touched. The cache never holds a stale value, but it can hold stale *memory* — exactly the gap the follow-up closes. |
| Clock jumps backwards | Entries appear to un-expire. Use a monotonic clock (`Environment.TickCount64`, not `DateTime.Now`). |
| Concurrent `Get` on the same key | Two threads can both decide an entry is expired and both unlink it, corrupting the list. Needs a lock; see the follow-up. |

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Write the interface and the two field declarations yourself; ask only for the method bodies.
- For TTL: "Add per-entry TTL using the injected IClock. Do not change eviction. List the members that change first."
- For threads: use the concurrency template — ask for the breaking interleaving, then decide the boundary yourself.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe a Dictionary of linked-list nodes plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) Get and Put, and an absolute expiry time per node makes TTL a single comparison. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Get and Put concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: LruTtlCache must be safe when many threads call Get and Put at once. Count must never exceed capacity and no value may be torn. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Swapping in `ConcurrentDictionary` and calling it thread-safe (R3).
- Get not moving the node to the front (R1) — passes put/get tests, fails eviction-after-read.
- TTL with expired entries left in place: returns -1 correctly, leaks memory, and evicts live entries first (R2).
- `DateTime.Now` instead of an injected clock — tests then need `Thread.Sleep`.
- A full-map sweep under the lock (R10).

**Verification exercise:** Memory leak — Expired entries are **never removed**: Get returns -1 but leaves them in the map and list. They count toward capacity, so the next Put evicts a *live* LRU entry while the dead one stays. Keys that are never read again stay forever — unbounded growth in a long-running process.

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Two threads call Get on different keys at once. What shared state do they touch?* — Both move nodes in one list: map + list invariant → one critical section
- *Lock or ConcurrentDictionary?* — Lock — the invariant spans two structures
- *Can this deadlock? Can the lock become a bottleneck?* — One lock, no callouts → no deadlock; yes under contention → shard

Shared state: the map and the list. The invariant spans both, so they must change together — one critical section per operation. Two threads in Get on different keys both call `_order.Remove` and `AddFirst`; without a lock the list's internal pointers interleave and corrupt. That is exactly what review exercise R3 does in 20/20 trials.

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *100× traffic, one hot key.* — Shard by hash; hot key still one shard → front cache or approximate recency
- *Memory pressure.* — Byte-weighted capacity; Resize down

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *What do you measure and alert on?* — Hit ratio (relative drop), evictions by reason, lock wait, size
- *The source behind it goes down.* — Serve stale with a bound, circuit breaker, collapse concurrent misses
- *What happens during a deploy?* — Cold cache → stampede on the source; warm up or ramp traffic

- Bound memory: capacity in entries is not bytes — for variable-size values, cap by weight.
- Hit ratio, eviction rate, expired-on-read rate as metrics; alert on hit-ratio drop.
- A slow source behind the cache: collapse concurrent misses (cache the in-flight `Lazy`), and add a timeout.
- Warm-up after deploy: a cold cache is a thundering herd on the source.

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**How would you handle cleanup of expired entries without impacting get() latency?**

Keep lazy expiry exactly as it is — it is what guarantees correctness — and add a **bounded background sweep** for reclamation. A min-heap keyed on expiry time gives the sweeper the next entry to die in O(1) peek, so a sweep that finds nothing due costs one comparison. Each sweep takes a budget, so one pass can never stall the process.

The subtlety is that a re-`Put` renews the TTL, which leaves a stale record in the heap pointing at an entry that is no longer due. Removing from a heap by key is O(n), so do not: give each entry a **version** and let the sweeper discard any record whose version no longer matches. Stale records cost memory until they surface, and nothing else.

*Trade-off:* Three options, and the right answer names all three.

**Lazy only** — zero background cost, `Get` stays O(1), but memory is held by dead entries until they are touched or evicted. Fine when capacity is the binding constraint anyway, which for a fixed-size cache it usually is.

**Lazy plus a bounded sweep** — memory is reclaimed promptly, `Get` is untouched, and the cost is one heap entry per `Put` plus the version field. This is the answer I would give.

**A timing wheel** — buckets of entries by coarse expiry slot, O(1) insert with no heap and no comparisons. Better than the heap when TTLs are few and similar (all 30 seconds, say), because then a bucket per second is cheap and exact. Worse when TTLs are arbitrary and wide, because you either get poor granularity or a huge wheel. Naming *when* it wins is the point; naming it as a buzzword is not.

**Make it thread-safe. What exactly are you protecting?**

A single lock around the whole operation is the correct first answer, and it is not a cop-out: the critical section is a handful of pointer writes, so contention is short even if it is frequent. `ConcurrentDictionary` alone is **not** enough and claiming it is would be the actual mistake.

If measurement says the lock is the bottleneck, the standard escape is sharding: N independent caches, each with its own lock, keyed by `hash(key) % N`. Recency then becomes per-shard rather than global, which is a real semantic change — you are no longer evicting the globally least-recently-used entry. Most production caches accept that trade; say that you know you are making it.

*Trade-off:* One lock: simple, obviously correct, serialises every operation including reads. Sharded locks: near-linear read scaling, approximate LRU. Lock-free: the recency list makes it very hard, and the usual production answer is to abandon strict LRU for something sampled — which is what Redis actually does, and it is worth knowing that the industry chose approximation here.

**The cache is distributed across many nodes now. What changes?**

Partition by key with consistent hashing, and make each node an independent local cache of exactly this design. Recency becomes per-node. TTL, on the other hand, travels very well: it is an absolute timestamp, needs no coordination, and every node can decide expiry alone — provided clocks are reasonably synchronised, which for second-scale TTLs they are.

*Trade-off:* You lose global LRU and gain linear scale. You also gain a new failure mode: on a topology change, keys move and a moved key’s TTL must be interpreted against the new node’s clock. Absolute expiries survive that; remaining-time TTLs do not — which retroactively justifies storing `ExpiresAt` rather than `ttl` in the node.

**Why not just use MemoryCache, or Redis with EXPIRE?**

`MemoryCache` gives absolute and sliding expiry and a size limit already. Redis gives `EXPIRE` plus `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`. Either removes the need for this code. I would reach for one of them unless I needed behaviour they do not offer — a custom eviction key, a specific memory shape, or no dependency.

*Trade-off:* Building it costs a day and owns a bug surface forever. Adopting one costs a dependency and gives up control of the eviction policy. What I would not do is build it *and* pretend the library does not exist — the interview answer and the production answer are allowed to differ, as long as you say which one you are giving.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Capacity 0? Re-put of an existing key? Get on a key that expired exactly now?* — Reject 0 at construction; update in place + renew; now == expiry is expired

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Complexity of Get, Put and the sweep?* — O(1), O(1), O(budget) — and why the sweep is bounded
- *Where is the bottleneck?* — Not the algorithm — the single lock

learn.title: 17 · Reference solution

designClaim: a Dictionary of linked-list nodes plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) Get and Put, and an absolute expiry time per node makes TTL a single comparison
